task: Write and maintain a project CHANGELOG.md that follows the Keep a Changelog 1.1.0 convention — adding entries for merged changes, cutting a release section, or repairing an existing changelog.
when_to_use: A change has landed and needs a changelog entry
Cutting/tagging a release and promoting Unreleased into a versioned section
Starting a CHANGELOG.md for a project that has none
Reviewing or repairing an existing changelog for format and completeness
Someone asks to turn a git log, diff, or PR list into release notes
source_attribution: Method from Keep a Changelog 1.1.0 by Olivier Lacan, MIT licensed. Compiled into a skill by the creator; interview-origin rules are the creator's additions.

procedure.text: Determine the mode: new changelog, add entry, cut release, or repair existing.

If the changelog does not exist, create CHANGELOG.md with the standard preamble ('All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.') plus links to Keep a Changelog and the project's versioning scheme, then an ## [Unreleased] section.
For each change, decide whether it is notable to a user of the project. Trivial internal churn is excluded; anything a consumer could observe is included.
Classify each notable change into exactly one of the six categories: Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, Security.
Write the entry as a human-readable sentence describing user-visible impact, not the code change.
Place entries under ## [Unreleased] until release; at release, rename that section to ## [X.Y.Z] - YYYY-MM-DD and open a fresh empty ## [Unreleased].
Maintain link-reference definitions at the bottom: each version links to its tag-comparison URL, Unreleased compares the latest tag to HEAD.
Omit any category heading that has no entries.

rules.text: Changelogs are for humans, not machines. Every entry describes what changed for a person using the software.
There must be an entry for every single version.
The same types of changes are grouped together under a category heading.
Versions and sections must be linkable — use [x.y.z] bracket headings with link-reference definitions.
The latest version comes first; ordering is reverse chronological.
Every released version displays its release date.
State whether the project adheres to Semantic Versioning (or which scheme it uses) in the preamble.

Use exactly six categories and no others: Added (new features), Changed (changes to existing functionality), Deprecated (soon-to-be-removed features), Removed (now-removed features), Fixed (bug fixes), Security (vulnerabilities).
Keep an Unreleased section at the top so users can see what is coming and maintainers can promote it at release time.
Dates use ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD) — largest to smallest unit, no regional ambiguity.
The file is named CHANGELOG.md, uppercase, at the project root.
Deprecations, removals, and breaking changes must always be documented — it must be painfully clear when something will break, and a deprecation must ship in a release before the removal.
Rewriting a changelog to add missed releases or correct overlooked breaking changes is correct and encouraged, not a violation.
Omit empty category sections — they occupy space and create noise; readers assume missing sections had no notable changes.
Each entry ends with a period.

taboos.text: Never dump commit log diffs as a changelog. Commit logs are full of merge commits, obscure titles, and documentation churn; they record source evolution, not user-facing change.
Never document only some of the notable changes — a partial changelog can be as dangerous as no changelog.
Never use ambiguous regional date formats (MM/DD/YYYY, DD-MM-YYYY).
Never invent categories outside the six.
Never remove or break something without a prior Deprecated entry.

output_format.shape:
# Changelog

All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.

The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/),
and this project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html).

## [Unreleased]

## [1.1.0] - 2019-02-15

### Added

- Danish translation.

### Fixed

- Italian translation.

[unreleased]: https://github.com/owner/repo/compare/v1.1.0...HEAD
[1.1.0]: https://github.com/owner/repo/compare/v1.0.0...v1.1.0

examples.why: The bad example is a commit title: it names the branch and PR number, not what a user gains.

edge_cases.handling: ## [0.0.5] - 2014-12-13 [YANKED] — bracketed so it is both visible to humans and parseable.
Hard in general because formats and filenames vary widely; this format improves but does not guarantee parseability.

edge_cases.case: GitHub Releases instead of a file
edge_cases.handling: GitHub Releases produce a non-portable changelog visible only inside GitHub, are less discoverable than an uppercase root file, and lack commit-comparison links between releases.

gaps.gap: Notability threshold: the article says trivial changes need not appear but never defines the line between notable and trivial. This decides every single entry.

Missing-data behavior: given a raw git log/diff, the writer often cannot tell user-facing impact, and may not know the version number or release date. The article never says what to do when the input is insufficient.
Category tiebreaker: no rule for changes that fit two categories (a security fix that is also a bug fix; a breaking change that is a modification; a removal that is also a fix).

Entry voice and shape: tense, person, length, whether PR/issue links, author credits, or ticket IDs belong in an entry. The source's own changelog uses terse imperative sentences but never states this as a rule.
Refusal case: is there a situation where the right output is to decline to write entries at all (e.g. asked to auto-generate a changelog from commits wholesale)?
Audience calibration: internal/private app vs. public library — does the standard bend for a project with no external consumers?
